entry.summary: A protocol declaration has no universal performance penalty. Runtime cost depends on how values cross the boundary, what information the optimizer can see, how data is stored, and how much real work each operation performs. A concrete value, a generic parameter, and an existential can expose the same behavior through different representations. Compare those representations in an actual workload before redesigning an application around assumptions about dispatch.

entry.title: Refactoring a Swift Class Hierarchy into Protocols

link.title: Refactoring a Swift Class Hierarchy into Protocols

entry.content:
A useful refactor changes where behavior lives while preserving what callers can observe. Replacing class with protocol is not enough: initialization, shared state, effect ordering, and error behavior can all change accidentally during the move.

We will migrate a small exporter with a formatting subclass into a composed design. The safety net checks actual exported text and forbidden writes after validation failure, rather than freezing the old private call graph.

Establish a behavior worth preserving

The exporter accepts one or more nonempty lines. It formats them, then writes the complete result once. Invalid input must never reach storage. Storage errors must propagate without reporting success.

enum ExportFailure: Error, Equatable {
    case invalidInput
    case destinationUnavailable
}

protocol ExportWriting {
    func write(_ text: String) throws
}

final class ExportRecorder: ExportWriting {
    private(set) var texts: [String] = []
    var rejectsWrites = false

    func write(_ text: String) throws {
        guard !rejectsWrites else { throw ExportFailure.destinationUnavailable }
        texts.append(text)
    }
}

class LegacyLineExporter {
    private let destination: any ExportWriting

    init(destination: any ExportWriting) { self.destination = destination }

    func format(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.joined(separator: "\n")
    }

    final func export(_ lines: [String]) throws {
        guard !lines.isEmpty, lines.allSatisfy({ !$0.isEmpty }) else {
            throw ExportFailure.invalidInput
        }
        let text = format(lines)
        try destination.write(text)
    }
}

final class LegacyBulletExporter: LegacyLineExporter {
    override func format(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.map { "- " + $0 }.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

The base class is not inherently broken. It provides a clear workflow and one customization hook. The refactoring pressure appears when formatting should be reused by previews and unrelated exporters without inheriting the storage lifecycle.

Use that actual requirement to select the boundary. A protocol for the mutable recorder itself is unnecessary; the consumer needs the existing writing capability, not every method of the concrete test helper.

Characterize the existing public operation

let legacyDestination = ExportRecorder()
let legacyExporter: LegacyLineExporter = LegacyBulletExporter(destination: legacyDestination)
try legacyExporter.export(["One", "Two"])
assert(legacyDestination.texts == ["- One\n- Two"])
do {
    try legacyExporter.export(["One", ""])
    assertionFailure("An empty line must be rejected")
} catch {
    assert(error as? ExportFailure == .invalidInput)
}
assert(legacyDestination.texts == ["- One\n- Two"])

The second case matters because failure happens after inspecting at least one valid line. The assertion establishes that rejected input does not produce a partial export.

The test uses a base-typed reference, which exercises the substitution path existing callers use. A test calling only the subclass’s format method would miss sequencing and validation behavior in export.

If the old behavior is itself a bug, record the intended change separately. A structural refactor and a product-rule change are easier to review when their effects are distinguishable.

Extract the varying calculation

protocol ExportFormatting {
    func format(_ lines: [String]) -> String
}

struct PlainExportFormat: ExportFormatting {
    func format(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

struct BulletExportFormat: ExportFormatting {
    func format(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.map { "- " + $0 }.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

struct ComposedLineExporter<F: ExportFormatting> {
    let formatter: F
    let destination: any ExportWriting

    func export(_ lines: [String]) throws {
        guard !lines.isEmpty, lines.allSatisfy({ !$0.isEmpty }) else {
            throw ExportFailure.invalidInput
        }
        let text = formatter.format(lines)
        try destination.write(text)
    }
}

Formatting is now a capability with value implementations. The exporter still reads as one workflow. The destination remains a separately owned effect, and formatting does not gain a storage dependency.

The exporter is generic because its configured formatter type remains stable for that constructed value. An existential property would also be reasonable if runtime replacement or simpler non-generic storage were important. That representation decision is separate from extracting the capability.

Swift’s Protocols and Generics chapters describe the mechanics. The tests here establish whether the migration preserved the behavior that matters.

Run the same observations against the new design

let composedDestination = ExportRecorder()
let composedExporter = ComposedLineExporter(
    formatter: BulletExportFormat(), destination: composedDestination
)
try composedExporter.export(["One", "Two"])
assert(composedDestination.texts == legacyDestination.texts)
do {
    try composedExporter.export(["One", ""])
    assertionFailure("An empty line must still be rejected")
} catch {
    assert(error as? ExportFailure == .invalidInput)
}
assert(composedDestination.texts == ["- One\n- Two"])

legacyDestination.rejectsWrites = true
composedDestination.rejectsWrites = true
do {
    try legacyExporter.export(["Three"])
    assertionFailure("The legacy write should fail")
} catch {
    assert(error as? ExportFailure == .destinationUnavailable)
}
do {
    try composedExporter.export(["Three"])
    assertionFailure("The composed write should fail")
} catch {
    assert(error as? ExportFailure == .destinationUnavailable)
}
assert(composedDestination.texts == legacyDestination.texts)

These assertions compare observable outcomes across both designs. They do not require the new exporter to call an inherited hook, preserve a private method name, or construct the same object graph.

The recorder fails before appending. A real destination might have more complicated partial-failure semantics. If the contract requires atomic replacement, name that requirement and test the infrastructure implementation rather than assuming this fake proves it.

Migrate consumers incrementally

A preview can now use BulletExportFormat directly without constructing a storage collaborator. The existing export use case can move to ComposedLineExporter at its composition root.

For a large codebase, the old base API can temporarily forward to the extracted formatter, preserving callers while migration proceeds. Keep that adapter behaviorally narrow; avoid turning it into another permanent abstraction layer without a consumer need.

Remove the old hierarchy only when references and tests show that no caller depends on it. Renaming files and deleting a superclass before understanding external subclass clients can create a source compatibility break even when local tests pass.

Preserve ownership, not just strings

In this example, both exporters retain their destinations. If several exporters should share one audit or store, assembly can pass the same instance. If they need independent state, construct separate owners.

Moving inherited instance storage into a global singleton changes sharing. Constructing a new helper inside every call changes lifetime in the opposite direction. Either can alter caching, metrics, or resource cleanup without changing one line of formatted output.

Document which collaborators are shared across features, scoped to an account, or fresh per operation. A protocol makes those objects replaceable; it does not choose their ownership graph.

Watch the frequency and order of effects

The old exporter validates, formats once, and writes once. A migration that moves formatting into a per-line storage loop can preserve simple output while changing effect count and partial-failure behavior.

If a hook reads time or random values, extracting it into a repeatedly invoked policy can change results too. Take one observation where the use case requires one observation, then pass that value into the calculation.

An algorithm’s meaningful ordering should remain visible in tests. Here the forbidden-write assertion protects validation-before-storage. If success notification were added, test that it happens only after a successful write.

Decide when the protocol is no longer needed

The new formatting boundary is justified by several implementations and independent preview use. If the final product has only one small pure format, a concrete formatter may be enough. Composition can remain useful without existential dispatch or a public protocol.

Conversely, a plugin API allowing implementations from another module may need a carefully documented public protocol and compatibility plan. The same source-level pattern serves different responsibilities depending on its consumers.

Finish with a change scenario

Add a numbered format. It should require a new formatting implementation and an assembly choice, while the stable export sequence remains unchanged. Then add a new validation rule, such as a maximum number of lines. That should change the workflow’s input policy and its tests rather than every formatter.

These changes provide evidence that responsibilities became more local. Counting the number of protocols or celebrating the absence of inheritance would not establish that benefit.

As a final exercise, add a shared contract test function that runs valid input and invalid input against both the old and new public entry points. Keep the negative control of a destination that throws. The migration is complete when intended behavior, errors, and lifetime are preserved and the new boundary makes a real consumer simpler.

Worked shared safety net: one contract, two constructions

Turn the migration observations into a reusable check whose negative control proves it can detect changed output:

func followsExportContract(
    make: (ExportRecorder) -> (([String]) throws -> Void)
) -> Bool {
    let destination = ExportRecorder()
    let export = make(destination)
    let expected = ["- One\n- Two"]
    do { try export(["One", "Two"]) } catch { return false }
    guard destination.texts == expected else { return false }
    do {
        try export([""])
        return false
    } catch ExportFailure.invalidInput {} catch { return false }
    guard destination.texts == expected else { return false }
    destination.rejectsWrites = true
    do {
        try export(["Three"])
        return false
    } catch ExportFailure.destinationUnavailable {} catch { return false }
    return destination.texts == expected
}

assert(followsExportContract { destination in
    LegacyBulletExporter(destination: destination).export
})
assert(followsExportContract { destination in
    ComposedLineExporter(formatter: BulletExportFormat(), destination: destination).export
})
assert(!followsExportContract { destination in
    { _ in try destination.write("Wrong output") }
})

The injected factory returns the operation under test, so the contract check is independent of the old and new concrete exporter types. Each run gets a fresh recorder and does not inherit state from another implementation’s test.

The check protects text, validation-before-write, and failure propagation. It intentionally does not assert that the implementation contains a protocol or avoids a superclass. Architecture is being judged by preserved behavior and a useful new boundary, not by a syntax test.

For a large migration, keep this contract while moving one construction site at a time. A compatibility adapter can delegate to the new implementation and run through the same check. Once all consumers have moved, remove the obsolete class hierarchy and adapter together if neither serves a remaining external client.

The negative control is small but important: a test suite that never demonstrates failure can give false confidence during a broad refactor. Here a wrong result is rejected immediately, before the failure-path checks even begin.

The safety net checks actual exported text and forbidden writes after validation failure, rather than freezing the old private call graph.

entry.title: Build a Small Reading-List App with Protocol-Oriented Swift

link.title: Build a Small Reading-List App with Protocol-Oriented Swift

entry.content:
A useful protocol-oriented example should do more than print two interchangeable greetings. It should own state, reject invalid input, perform a replaceable effect, and behave predictably when that effect fails.

This reading-list feature adds books and toggles their read status. A SwiftUI screen renders one model, a small storage protocol isolates persistence, and value snapshots keep proposed changes separate from accepted state. The complete examples target Swift 6 and a modern SwiftUI toolchain.

State the product rules first

A new item needs a nonblank title. Every item has a stable identifier independent of its title. Toggling one item must not change another. A failed save must preserve the list the user previously saw, and the input should remain available for another attempt.

These rules tell us where boundaries belong. Titles and item snapshots are values. One observable model owns the screen’s current state. Storage is a capability because production and tests need different effects. Identifier creation is a function because it is one source of nondeterminism.

This is a complete small feature, with a runnable in-memory store and a SwiftUI screen. Disk persistence is an adapter exercise rather than an untested network call hidden behind a synchronous signature.

Keep the domain values concrete

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct ReadingItem: Identifiable, Equatable {
    let id: UUID
    let title: String
    var isRead: Bool
}

struct ReadingListState: Equatable {
    var items: [ReadingItem] = []
    var message: String?
    var loaded = false
}

An item does not need a protocol merely because the feature uses protocol-oriented design elsewhere. Its concrete fields already form a useful snapshot.

Identity uses a UUID, so two books with the same title can remain distinct. Equality compares the whole snapshot, including read status. That separates “the same list row” from “the same current content.”

The state contains values rather than mutable service references. Copying a proposed item array therefore preserves the observable independence needed before a save is accepted.

Define the persistence guarantee the model needs

@MainActor
protocol ReadingListStoring: AnyObject {
    func load() throws -> [ReadingItem]
    // A failed replacement must preserve the previously stored list.
    func replace(_ items: [ReadingItem]) throws
}

enum ReadingStoreFailure: Error { case unavailable }

@MainActor
final class MemoryReadingStore: ReadingListStoring {
    private var items: [ReadingItem]
    var rejectsWrites = false
    private(set) var writeAttempts = 0

    init(items: [ReadingItem] = []) { self.items = items }
    func load() -> [ReadingItem] { items }

    func replace(_ proposed: [ReadingItem]) throws {
        writeAttempts += 1
        guard !rejectsWrites else { throw ReadingStoreFailure.unavailable }
        items = proposed
    }
}

The store deliberately exposes a whole-list replacement. That makes the model’s transaction boundary small and explicit. A real file adapter might encode the snapshot and use an atomic replacement operation; it must honor the same failure guarantee.

Main-actor isolation fits this in-memory UI example. Do not implement blocking remote or large disk operations under this synchronous interface. An asynchronous storage contract needs additional loading, cancellation, and stale-result rules, while the value snapshots can remain useful.

The fault switch is specific to the teaching store. It makes a failure deterministic without changing global state or waiting for a server to fail.

Let one model own accepted state

@MainActor
final class ReadingListModel: ObservableObject {
    @Published private(set) var state = ReadingListState()
    private let store: any ReadingListStoring
    private let nextID: () -> UUID

    init(store: any ReadingListStoring, nextID: @escaping () -> UUID = UUID.init) {
        self.store = store
        self.nextID = nextID
    }

    func loadIfNeeded() {
        guard !state.loaded else { return }
        do {
            let items = try store.load()
            guard Set(items.map(\.id)).count == items.count else {
                state.message = "The saved list contains duplicate identifiers"
                return
            }
            state = ReadingListState(items: items, message: nil, loaded: true)
        } catch {
            state.message = "Could not load your reading list"
        }
    }

    func add(title: String) {
        guard state.loaded else {
            state.message = "Load the reading list first"
            return
        }
        let cleaned = title.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !cleaned.isEmpty else {
            state.message = "Enter a title"
            return
        }
        let id = nextID()
        guard !state.items.contains(where: { $0.id == id }) else {
            state.message = "Could not create a unique item"
            return
        }
        save(state.items + [ReadingItem(id: id, title: cleaned, isRead: false)])
    }

    func toggle(id: UUID) {
        guard state.loaded else { return }
        guard let index = state.items.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == id }) else {
            state.message = "This item is no longer available"
            return
        }
        var proposed = state.items
        proposed[index].isRead.toggle()
        save(proposed)
    }

    private func save(_ proposed: [ReadingItem]) {
        do {
            try store.replace(proposed)
            state = ReadingListState(items: proposed, message: nil, loaded: true)
        } catch {
            state.message = "Could not save that change"
        }
    }
}

The model calculates a proposed list, asks storage to accept it, then publishes the new snapshot. Failure updates only the message. It does not leave a toggled in-memory row that disagrees with storage.

loadIfNeeded avoids resetting accepted state on repeated SwiftUI appearances. A failed initial load can be retried because loaded remains false. Duplicate saved identifiers are rejected before the list is accepted, protecting the identity assumption the UI relies on.

Identifier generation is injected so tests can reproduce exact items. The duplicate check also establishes a defined failure if a faulty generator returns an existing ID. A UUID makes collisions unlikely; it does not justify leaving the model’s invariants undefined.

Give SwiftUI a rendering role

struct ReadingListScreen: View {
    @ObservedObject var model: ReadingListModel
    @State private var newTitle = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            HStack {
                TextField("Book title", text: $newTitle)
                Button("Add") {
                    model.add(title: newTitle)
                    if model.state.message == nil { newTitle = "" }
                }
                .disabled(!model.state.loaded)
            }
            List(model.state.items) { item in
                HStack {
                    Text(item.title)
                    Spacer()
                    Button(item.isRead ? "Mark unread" : "Mark read") {
                        model.toggle(id: item.id)
                    }
                }
            }
            if let message = model.state.message {
                Text(message).foregroundStyle(.red)
                if !model.state.loaded {
                    Button("Retry loading") { model.loadIfNeeded() }
                }
            }
        }
        .padding()
        .task { model.loadIfNeeded() }
    }
}

struct ReadingListRoot: View {
    @StateObject private var model: ReadingListModel

    @MainActor
    init(store: any ReadingListStoring) {
        _model = StateObject(wrappedValue: ReadingListModel(store: store))
    }

    var body: some View { ReadingListScreen(model: model) }
}

The root establishes observable-object ownership with StateObject. The child observes the supplied model. Constructing a fresh model inside the child’s body would risk resetting state when SwiftUI reevaluates the view hierarchy.

The screen keeps unsaved text in local State. It clears that text only after the model reports a successful operation. A failed save leaves the input available, matching the stated product rule.

The UI does not know whether storage is a dictionary, a file, or a test recorder. It also does not navigate through a service locator to discover dependencies during rendering.

Assemble a preview with an explicit lifetime

At the application’s composition root, construct one MemoryReadingStore and pass it to ReadingListRoot(store:). Place that root in your app’s window or navigation flow. Its StateObject keeps the model stable for that root’s identity.

The memory store intentionally loses data when that owner disappears. That is suitable for a preview or a test, not durable storage. A production adapter can preserve the same whole-list contract while adding encoding and atomic file replacement.

Do not make the store a global singleton simply to preserve data across view recreation. Persistence lifetime and view lifetime are different concerns. Decide which owner retains the store and where the durable data lives.

flowchart TB
    accTitle: Reading-list feature responsibilities
    accDescr: A SwiftUI root owns the model. The screen sends commands and observes value state. The model depends on storage and identifier creation.
    Root[ReadingListRoot] --> Model[ReadingListModel]
    Screen[ReadingListScreen] -->|commands| Model
    Model -->|value state| Screen
    Model --> Store[ReadingListStoring]
    Model --> IDs[Identifier function]
    Store -.-> Memory[Memory or file adapter]

Test without launching the UI

@MainActor
func checkReadingListFeature() throws {
    let firstID = UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001")!
    let secondID = UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002")!
    var identifiers = [firstID, secondID].makeIterator()
    let store = MemoryReadingStore()
    let model = ReadingListModel(store: store, nextID: { identifiers.next()! })

    model.loadIfNeeded()
    assert(model.state.loaded)
    model.add(title: "  Protocols  ")
    assert(model.state.items == [ReadingItem(id: firstID, title: "Protocols", isRead: false)])
    assert(store.writeAttempts == 1)

    model.add(title: " \n ")
    assert(model.state.message == "Enter a title")
    assert(store.writeAttempts == 1)

    model.toggle(id: firstID)
    assert(model.state.items[0].isRead)
    let beforeFailure = model.state.items
    store.rejectsWrites = true
    model.toggle(id: firstID)
    assert(model.state.items == beforeFailure)
    assert(model.state.message == "Could not save that change")
    let storedAfterFailure = try store.load()
    assert(storedAfterFailure == beforeFailure)

    store.rejectsWrites = false
    model.add(title: "Generics")
    assert(model.state.items.map(\.id) == [firstID, secondID])
    assert(model.state.message == nil)
    model.loadIfNeeded()
    assert(model.state.items.count == 2)
}
try checkReadingListFeature()

The test controls identity and failure directly. It proves validation prevents a storage attempt, a rejected save preserves both visible and stored state, and a later valid change can recover.

The finite identifier iterator is a focused test fixture. Its forced unwrap represents the test’s known number of ID requests; production construction uses UUID generation. If the model unexpectedly creates another identifier, the fixture fails rather than quietly masking that interaction change.

Extend the adapter boundary carefully

A file store should test missing files, corrupted data, duplicate IDs, encoding failure, and replacement failure. Decide whether a missing file means an empty initial list or an error; the adapter must implement the chosen policy consistently.

For multiple simultaneous editors, whole-list replacement can overwrite another editor’s changes. Add a revision token and conditional save when that is a real requirement. A protocol does not make read-modify-write sequences transactional across independently loaded owners.

For asynchronous storage, accept or reject late outcomes according to a request generation or operation identifier. Cancelling a task may not prevent a completion already in flight. Keep the model’s acceptance rule separate from the transport’s cancellation mechanism.

Evaluate what POP contributed

The storage protocol isolates an effect and makes a failure controllable. The model remains a concrete class because it owns observable identity and state. Items remain concrete values because independent proposals and comparisons matter. Identifier creation remains a small function because a larger service interface would add little.

There is no protocol for the view, item, state, or model merely for consistency. Each abstraction has a consumer and an observable benefit.

As an exercise, add deletion with the same save-before-publish rule. Test deleting an unknown identifier, a failed deletion save, and deleting one of two identically titled items. The stable ID should determine which item changes. If that extension can be understood without rewriting the storage and presentation boundaries, the design is doing useful work.

Worked extension: delete by identity with the same commit rule

Deletion can reuse the model’s existing save boundary. Place this extension in the same file as the model so it can access that model’s private save operation:

extension ReadingListModel {
    func remove(id: UUID) {
        guard state.loaded else { return }
        guard state.items.contains(where: { $0.id == id }) else {
            state.message = "This item is no longer available"
            return
        }
        save(state.items.filter { $0.id != id })
    }
}

@MainActor
func checkReadingListDeletion() throws {
    let first = UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000011")!
    let second = UUID(uuidString: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000012")!
    let originals = [
        ReadingItem(id: first, title: "Same title", isRead: false),
        ReadingItem(id: second, title: "Same title", isRead: true)
    ]
    let store = MemoryReadingStore(items: originals)
    let model = ReadingListModel(store: store)
    model.loadIfNeeded()
    store.rejectsWrites = true
    model.remove(id: first)
    assert(model.state.items == originals)
    let unchangedStorage = try store.load()
    assert(unchangedStorage == originals)

    store.rejectsWrites = false
    model.remove(id: first)
    assert(model.state.items == [originals[1]])
    let attempts = store.writeAttempts
    model.remove(id: first)
    assert(store.writeAttempts == attempts)
    assert(model.state.items == [originals[1]])
}
try checkReadingListDeletion()

The two items share a title, so a title-based removal would be ambiguous. Stable identity selects exactly one row. A rejected save leaves both rows present; a repeated removal reports absence without another write attempt.

The SwiftUI row can call remove(id:) from a delete control. Pass the item’s identifier rather than a retained array index. An index captured before another edit may refer to a different item later, while the identifier expresses the intended entity.

A duplicate-ID load is a different failure. The model rejects that saved list before enabling editing because it cannot safely identify individual rows. A production adapter should also validate its decoded schema, but the model’s check preserves the invariant at the point the UI accepts the data.

No new storage protocol or factory was needed for deletion. The existing whole-list replacement already matches the feature’s transaction boundary. That is a useful test of the design: a related command reuses an honest capability without inventing a new layer merely to represent another button.

It should own state, reject invalid input, perform a replaceable effect, and behave predictably when that effect fails. This reading-list feature adds books and toggles their read status. A SwiftUI screen renders one model, a small storage protocol isolates persistence, and value snapshots keep proposed changes separate from accepted state. The complete examples target Swift 6 and a modern SwiftUI toolchain.

entry.title: Factories in Protocol-Oriented Swift: Construct the Right Capability

link.title: Factories in Protocol-Oriented Swift: Construct the Right Capability

entry.content:
A factory decides how to construct a useful object or value. In protocol-oriented Swift, it can return a capability rather than expose the concrete implementation chosen by configuration.

That does not require a factory class hierarchy. A function, enum switch, or injected creation closure is often enough. The important decisions are what varies, when construction can fail, and whether each call produces a fresh resource or returns shared state.

Begin with the consumer’s operation

protocol LineExporting {
    func export(_ lines: [String]) -> String
}

struct PlainLineExporter: LineExporting {
    func export(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

struct BulletLineExporter: LineExporting {
    func export(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.map { "• " + $0 }.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

enum LineExportFormat: String {
    case plain
    case bullets
}

func makeLineExporter(format: LineExportFormat) -> any LineExporting {
    switch format {
    case .plain: return PlainLineExporter()
    case .bullets: return BulletLineExporter()
    }
}

let plainLineExporter = makeLineExporter(format: .plain)
let bulletLineExporter = makeLineExporter(format: .bullets)
assert(plainLineExporter.export(["A", "B"]) == "A\nB")
assert(bulletLineExporter.export(["A", "B"]) == "• A\n• B")

The enum represents a closed configuration choice. The factory returns an existential because runtime configuration can choose unrelated conforming types. The consumer uses only exporting behavior.

There is no need for PlainExporterFactory, BulletExporterFactory, and an abstract factory superclass just to move this small switch into three files. Add more structure when construction itself has meaningful independent variation.

Validate external configuration before constructing

enum ExportConfigurationFailure: Error, Equatable {
    case unsupportedFormat(String)
}

func configuredLineExporter(name: String) throws -> any LineExporting {
    guard let format = LineExportFormat(rawValue: name) else {
        throw ExportConfigurationFailure.unsupportedFormat(name)
    }
    return makeLineExporter(format: format)
}

let configuredBulletExporter = try configuredLineExporter(name: "bullets")
assert(configuredBulletExporter.export(["Ready"]) == "• Ready")
do {
    _ = try configuredLineExporter(name: "unknown")
    assertionFailure("Unknown configuration must be reported")
} catch {
    assert(error as? ExportConfigurationFailure == .unsupportedFormat("unknown"))
}

Silently choosing plain output for every unknown string would hide a configuration mistake. A fallback is valid only if the product explicitly defines that behavior and callers can rely on it.

The configuration parser belongs at the boundary receiving the string. Inside the feature, the enum carries the validated choice. This avoids spreading string comparisons and default branches through every consumer.

The Swift guide’s Opaque and Boxed Protocol Types explains why an existential can represent runtime variation that an ordinary opaque return cannot express across unrelated underlying types.

A factory and its product have different lifetimes

An editing feature needs a fresh session for each opened document. Reusing a singleton session would let one editor overwrite another editor’s draft.

final class DraftEditSession {
    let id: Int
    var text: String

    init(id: Int, text: String) {
        self.id = id
        self.text = text
    }
}

protocol DraftSessionMaking {
    func makeSession(text: String) -> DraftEditSession
}

final class DraftSessionFactory: DraftSessionMaking {
    private var nextID = 0

    func makeSession(text: String) -> DraftEditSession {
        nextID += 1
        return DraftEditSession(id: nextID, text: text)
    }
}

struct DraftOpening {
    let factory: any DraftSessionMaking

    func open(_ text: String) -> DraftEditSession {
        factory.makeSession(text: text)
    }
}

let draftSessionFactory = DraftSessionFactory()
let draftOpening = DraftOpening(factory: draftSessionFactory)
let firstDraftSession = draftOpening.open("First")
let secondDraftSession = draftOpening.open("Second")
firstDraftSession.text = "Edited first"
assert(firstDraftSession !== secondDraftSession)
assert(firstDraftSession.id != secondDraftSession.id)
assert(secondDraftSession.text == "Second")

The application can retain one factory while consumers own separate products. The factory’s counter is an intentionally local identifier source for this serialized example, not a durable cross-launch document identifier.

A production resource factory may need to throw while opening a file or transaction. The product owner then needs an explicit close, cancel, or commit lifecycle. Returning a protocol capability does not make resource acquisition or cleanup disappear.

Inject a factory when creation is the variation

Injecting an already created session would force the feature to reuse that session. Injecting a factory lets the feature request fresh state when an operation begins. These dependencies express different lifetime policies.

For one simple creation operation, a closure such as (String) -> DraftEditSession can be sufficient. A named protocol becomes useful when it documents an important capability, groups related creation operations, or carries associated type relationships.

Avoid replacing specific factory dependencies with a generic service locator. A feature that receives resolve(Type.self) can discover arbitrary dependencies at runtime, hiding what construction and execution actually require. makeSession(text:) is a clear operation with a clear product.

Choose concrete, generic, opaque, or existential results deliberately

A factory returning DraftEditSession is honest when every supported product is that concrete session type. It still supplies a fresh instance and centralizes construction; factories do not require existential returns.

A generic factory parameter is useful when the caller chooses a product family and the type relationship must remain visible. An opaque result hides one underlying implementation chosen by a declaration. An existential result can choose among conformers at runtime.

Do not return Self merely to make a factory look flexible. In a non-final class hierarchy, constructing dynamic Self can impose a required initializer contract on every subclass. A separate factory often avoids forcing unrelated construction needs into one inherited initializer.

Keep assembly near the application boundary

flowchart LR
    accTitle: Factory selection stays in assembly
    accDescr: Configuration selects a factory result, which is supplied as an exporting capability to the feature. The feature does not inspect concrete exporter types.
    Config[Validated configuration] --> Factory[makeLineExporter]
    Factory --> Exporter[LineExporting implementation]
    Exporter --> Feature[Export feature]

The feature should not repeatedly inspect configuration and rebuild its dependencies during every operation unless runtime replacement is an actual requirement. Stable constructor injection gives it a valid collaborator for its intended lifetime.

A composition root can assemble an application-wide transport, an account-scoped repository, and a fresh edit session. Those scopes are decisions about reuse and ownership. Factory syntax makes the decisions visible; it does not choose them automatically.

Test the products through their promised interfaces

For exporter selection, assert complete output for each configuration choice and a meaningful error for an unsupported external value. A test that checks only the product’s concrete type can pass while its behavior is wrong.

For session construction, assert distinct instance identity and independent mutation. Also test whether required collaborators are intentionally shared between sessions. Two sessions can have independent draft text while reporting to the same audit service; that is a valid graph if documented.

For failing resource acquisition, verify that the factory returns no half-valid product and releases any resources acquired before the failure. A factory’s main benefit is delivering a usable product under a clear construction contract.

Avoid speculative registration systems

A dictionary of string names to arbitrary creation closures may be justified for plugins loaded independently. For two known export formats, an enum switch is easier to discover, validate, and exhaustively handle.

Registration introduces duplicate-name rules, missing registrations, initialization order, and a lifetime for the registry. Those are real costs. Do not add them simply because a pattern catalog calls factories extensible.

As an exercise, add a third exporter with an immutable separator configuration. Decide whether the configuration is part of the format enum’s associated data, a separate validated value, or a construction argument. Keep the consumer-facing exporting operation unchanged and test the configured output. The factory has earned its role when construction choices remain clear while the feature continues to depend on the capability it actually uses.

Worked extension: add a configured product without a factory hierarchy

The third format can carry immutable separator configuration while reusing the existing choices:

struct JoinedLineExporter: LineExporting {
    let separator: String
    func export(_ lines: [String]) -> String {
        lines.joined(separator: separator)
    }
}

enum ConfiguredExportChoice {
    case standard(LineExportFormat)
    case joined(separator: String)
}

func makeConfiguredExporter(_ choice: ConfiguredExportChoice) -> any LineExporting {
    switch choice {
    case let .standard(format): return makeLineExporter(format: format)
    case let .joined(separator): return JoinedLineExporter(separator: separator)
    }
}

let slashExporter = makeConfiguredExporter(.joined(separator: " / "))
let pipeExporter = makeConfiguredExporter(.joined(separator: " | "))
assert(slashExporter.export(["One", "Two"]) == "One / Two")
assert(pipeExporter.export(["One", "Two"]) == "One | Two")
assert(slashExporter.export([]) == "")
assert(makeConfiguredExporter(.standard(.plain)).export(["One", "Two"]) == "One\nTwo")

Each product retains its own configuration. Constructing the pipe exporter does not modify the slash exporter’s behavior. A mutable static separator would create hidden sharing and make these two simultaneous configurations harder to support.

The factory still has a small exhaustive switch. No registry or abstract factory family is necessary because the application owns these finite choices. Independent plugins could justify a different extension mechanism when they become a real requirement.

The separator is unrestricted in this rendering contract, including the empty string. If a target file format restricts separators or requires escaping, add those domain rules to a validated format value or a dedicated exporter. Joining strings is not automatically a compliant CSV encoder merely because the separator happens to be a comma.

The stable consumer operation remains export. Construction and format-specific policy changed locally, which is the concrete benefit the factory boundary was intended to provide.

entry.title: Clean Code in Swift
entry.content:
Clean code is code that the next person, often you in six months, can read, trust, and change without fear. Most clean code advice is language-agnostic, but Swift gives you unusually strong tools to apply it: API design guidelines built around the call site, value types, optionals, enums with associated values, access control, and a compiler that can rule out whole classes of mistakes, including data races. This article starts with a realistic refactoring, then goes through the habits that make the biggest difference in day-to-day Swift, the code smells to watch for, and where “clean” turns into over-engineering.

Clean Code in Swift

A refactoring, start to finish

Here’s a function of a kind that exists in many codebases. It works, and it’s tested by hand every release:

func price(_ items: [(String, Double, Int)], _ type: String, _ code: String?, _ express: Bool) -> Double {
    var t = 0.0
    for i in items {
        t += i.1 * Double(i.2)
    }
    if type == "gold" {
        t = t * 0.9
    } else {
        if type == "silver" {
            t = t * 0.95
        }
    }
    if code != nil {
        if code! == "WELCOME10" {
            t = t - 10
        }
    }
    if t < 0 { t = 0 }
    if express {
        t += 15
    } else {
        if t < 50 {
            t += 5
        }
    }
    return t
}

let legacyTotal = price([("Book", 20, 2), ("Pen", 2.5, 4)], "gold", "WELCOME10", false)
print(legacyTotal)   // 40.0

What makes it hard to work with:

  • The call site is unreadable. price(items, "gold", "WELCOME10", false): what’s false?
  • Stringly typed inputs. A typo like "Gold" silently means “no discount”.
  • Tuples with positional fields (i.1, i.2) hide meaning.
  • Magic numbers (0.9, 15, 50, 5) carry business rules nobody can find.
  • Nesting and a force-unwrap, and one function doing four jobs: subtotal, membership discount, coupons, shipping.

Here’s the same logic, refactored step by step into types that carry meaning:

struct LineItem {
    let name: String
    let unitPrice: Double
    let quantity: Int

    var total: Double { unitPrice * Double(quantity) }
}

enum Membership {
    case standard, silver, gold

    var discountRate: Double {
        switch self {
        case .standard: 0
        case .silver: 0.05
        case .gold: 0.10
        }
    }
}

enum Coupon: String {
    case welcome10 = "WELCOME10"

    var amountOff: Double {
        switch self {
        case .welcome10: 10
        }
    }
}

enum Shipping {
    case standard, express

    static let freeStandardThreshold = 50.0

    func cost(forSubtotal subtotal: Double) -> Double {
        switch self {
        case .express: 15
        case .standard: subtotal < Self.freeStandardThreshold ? 5 : 0
        }
    }
}

struct Checkout {
    let items: [LineItem]
    let membership: Membership
    let coupon: Coupon?
    let shipping: Shipping

    var total: Double {
        let discounted = subtotal * (1 - membership.discountRate)
        let afterCoupon = max(0, discounted - (coupon?.amountOff ?? 0))
        return afterCoupon + shipping.cost(forSubtotal: afterCoupon)
    }

    private var subtotal: Double {
        items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.total }
    }
}

let checkout = Checkout(
    items: [
        LineItem(name: "Book", unitPrice: 20, quantity: 2),
        LineItem(name: "Pen", unitPrice: 2.5, quantity: 4),
    ],
    membership: .gold,
    coupon: Coupon(rawValue: "WELCOME10"),
    shipping: .standard
)
print(checkout.total)   // 40.0

The result is longer, and that’s fine: clean doesn’t mean short. Every rule now has a name and a home. A typo in a membership level is a compile error. The call site documents itself. Adding a membership tier makes the compiler point at every switch that must handle it. And each piece can be tested on its own: Shipping.standard.cost(forSubtotal: 49) is a one-line test.

Before refactoring code like this for real, pin its current behavior with a few tests (including the odd cases, like a coupon larger than the subtotal), so you can prove the new version gives the same answers.

Names that read at the point of use

Swift’s API Design Guidelines put clarity at the point of use first. You write a declaration once, but it’s read at every call site:

struct Inbox {
    private(set) var messages: [String] = []

    // Reads as a phrase at the call site: inbox.insert(message, at: 0)
    mutating func insert(_ message: String, at index: Int) {
        messages.insert(message, at: index)
    }

    // Boolean properties read as assertions
    var isEmpty: Bool { messages.isEmpty }
}

var inbox = Inbox()
inbox.insert("Welcome!", at: 0)
print(inbox.isEmpty)   // false

The guidelines’ most useful rules in practice:

  • Name by role, not type. greeting, not string; messages, not messagesArray.
  • Omit needless words, but keep words that prevent ambiguity: remove(at: index) is clear; remove(index) could mean “remove the value index”.
  • Mutating and non-mutating pairs follow a pattern: verbs mutate, past participles return a new value: sort() / sorted(), append(_:) / appending(_:), normalize() / normalized().
  • Side-effect-free methods read as nouns (distance(to:)); methods with side effects read as verbs (print(_:), save()).
  • Factory methods start with make: makeIterator().
  • Protocols that describe what something is are nouns (Collection); capabilities end in -able, -ible, or -ing (Equatable, ProgressReporting).
  • Avoid abbreviations (usr, mgr, cfg) and vague words (data, info, manager, handle, process) that could mean anything.

For formatting and layout conventions, see Mastering Swift Style Guides.

Boolean parameters are a smell

render(true, false) tells the reader nothing. Swift’s argument labels help, but an enum is usually better still, because it can grow a third case later without changing every call site:

enum ImageQuality {
    case thumbnail, full
}

func loadImage(named name: String, quality: ImageQuality) -> String {
    switch quality {
    case .thumbnail: "\(name)@small"
    case .full: "\(name)@full"
    }
}

print(loadImage(named: "avatar", quality: .thumbnail))   // avatar@small

The same goes for long parameter lists: when a function takes six parameters, several of them usually belong together in a struct.

Small functions that do one thing

If a function needs comments to explain its sections, those sections probably want to be functions with names:

struct Order {
    var items: [Double]
    var couponPercent: Double
}

func total(for order: Order) -> Double {
    let subtotal = order.items.reduce(0, +)
    return applyDiscount(to: subtotal, percent: order.couponPercent)
}

private func applyDiscount(to amount: Double, percent: Double) -> Double {
    amount * (1 - percent / 100)
}

print(total(for: Order(items: [10, 30], couponPercent: 25)))   // 30.0

Each function has one reason to change, and its name tells you what it does without reading the body. A good test: can you describe the function in one sentence without “and”?

Flatten with guard

Deep nesting hides the main path. Check preconditions up front and exit early, so the happy path runs down the left margin:

struct SignUpForm {
    var email: String?
    var password: String?
    var acceptedTerms: Bool
}

enum SignUpError: Error {
    case missingEmail, weakPassword, termsNotAccepted
}

func validate(_ form: SignUpForm) throws(SignUpError) -> (email: String, password: String) {
    guard let email = form.email, !email.isEmpty else { throw .missingEmail }
    guard let password = form.password, password.count >= 8 else { throw .weakPassword }
    guard form.acceptedTerms else { throw .termsNotAccepted }
    return (email, password)
}

do {
    _ = try validate(SignUpForm(email: "sam@example.com", password: "short", acceptedTerms: true))
} catch {
    print(error)   // weakPassword
}

Each guard states one requirement, and the compiler guarantees its else branch leaves the scope. Swift 6’s typed throws let the caller know the exact set of failures; see Error Handling in Swift.

Make invalid states unrepresentable

Booleans and optionals that must be kept in sync are a bug waiting to happen:

// Which combinations are valid? isLoading == true with an error and items?
struct ScreenStateFlags {
    var isLoading: Bool
    var items: [String]?
    var error: Error?
}

// Exactly one state at a time, each with its own data
enum ScreenState {
    case loading
    case loaded([String])
    case failed(Error)
}

Three independent properties allow 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations, most of them nonsense; the enum allows exactly three. The enum version can’t be in a contradictory state, and every switch over it must handle all cases. See Enumerations in Swift.

Types instead of primitives

“Primitive obsession”, using String, Int, and Double for everything, lets you mix up values that happen to share a type. Small wrapper types cost nothing at runtime and turn mix-ups into compile errors:

struct UserID: Hashable {
    let rawValue: Int
}

struct OrderID: Hashable {
    let rawValue: Int
}

func cancel(_ order: OrderID, requestedBy user: UserID) -> String {
    "user \(user.rawValue) cancelled order \(order.rawValue)"
}

let user = UserID(rawValue: 7)
let order = OrderID(rawValue: 1_042)
print(cancel(order, requestedBy: user))   // user 7 cancelled order 1042
// cancel(order, requestedBy: order)      // ❌ compile error: an OrderID isn't a UserID

The same idea works for validated values. A failable initializer checks once, and every function that takes the type can rely on it:

struct EmailAddress {
    let value: String

    init?(_ candidate: String) {
        let parts = candidate.split(separator: "@")
        guard parts.count == 2, parts[1].contains(".") else { return nil }
        value = candidate
    }
}

print(EmailAddress("sam@example.com")?.value ?? "invalid")   // sam@example.com
print(EmailAddress("not-an-email")?.value ?? "invalid")      // invalid

A function that takes an EmailAddress instead of a String never needs to validate it again. That’s “parse, don’t validate”: convert untrusted input into a type that proves it’s valid at the boundary, then trust it everywhere inside.

Prefer values and let

  • Use let by default; switch to var only when something really changes. The compiler warns when a var is never mutated.
  • Prefer structs over classes, so data can’t change behind your back through another reference. See Structures and Classes.
  • Prefer non-mutating transformations for data flow:
let prices = [12.0, 7.5, 30.0]
let affordableWithTax = prices
    .filter { $0 < 20 }
    .map { $0 * 1.25 }
print(affordableWithTax)   // [15.0, 9.375]
  • When you do use classes, mark them final unless they’re designed for subclassing. It documents intent and enables static dispatch.

Don’t force-unwrap your way out

Every ! is a promise that something is never nil. Sometimes that’s genuinely true, like a URL built from a string literal you control, but usually it’s a crash waiting to happen. Use if let, guard let, ??, or a non-optional type instead:

let input = "4x2"
let quantity = Int(input) ?? 1          // explicit fallback
// let quantity = Int(input)!           // ❌ crashes on bad input
print(quantity)                         // 1

When a value truly can’t be nil because of an invariant, say so with a message, so the crash report explains itself: guard let url = URL(string: template) else { preconditionFailure("Invalid URL template: \(template)") }.

Hide what others shouldn’t touch

Start with the most restrictive access and widen only when needed. private and private(set) keep invariants in one place:

struct BankAccount {
    private(set) var balance = 0   // readable everywhere, writable only here

    mutating func deposit(_ amount: Int) {
        precondition(amount > 0, "Deposits must be positive")
        balance += amount
    }
}

var account = BankAccount()
account.deposit(50)
print(account.balance)   // 50
// account.balance = 1_000_000   // ❌ the setter is private

Organize each conformance in its own extension, with private helpers next to the code that uses them. It keeps files scannable and makes a type’s responsibilities visible at a glance; see Access Control and Extensions.

Depend on abstractions at the edges

Code that talks to the network, the database, the file system, or the clock is hard to test and hard to reason about. Put a small protocol in front of it, and inject the dependency:

import Foundation

protocol Clock {
    var now: Date { get }
}

struct SystemClock: Clock {
    var now: Date { Date() }
}

struct FixedClock: Clock {
    let now: Date
}

struct SessionValidator {
    let clock: any Clock

    func isExpired(_ expiry: Date) -> Bool {
        clock.now > expiry
    }
}

let expiry = Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 1_000)
let validator = SessionValidator(clock: FixedClock(now: Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 2_000)))
print(validator.isExpired(expiry))   // true, every time, on every machine

Production code passes SystemClock(); tests pass a fixed clock and get deterministic results. Keep the core logic pure (inputs in, outputs out) and push side effects to the edges: pure code is trivial to test and impossible to break through hidden state. Test Doubles in Swift shows this pattern in depth.

Handle errors honestly

  • Throw descriptive errors instead of returning nil when the caller needs to know why something failed.
  • Never silently swallow errors with an empty catch {}; at minimum, log them.
  • Translate low-level errors at module boundaries, so UI code doesn’t switch over URLError codes.
  • Reserve fatalError and precondition for programmer errors, never for user input or network failures.

Comments explain why

Code says what it does; comments should say what code can’t:

// The payments API caches responses for up to 5 minutes after a change,
// so we bypass the cache right after the user edits their card.
let shouldBypassCache = true

Documentation comments (///) show up in Xcode’s Quick Help and in DocC, so use them for public APIs: what the function does, its parameters, what it throws, and any complexity guarantees. Delete commented-out code (version control remembers it), and use // MARK: - to organize long files into sections that appear in Xcode’s jump bar.

A catalog of Swift code smells

Smell Usually means Try
A 1,000-line view controller Too many responsibilities Extract views, view models, and services
func f(_: Bool, _: Bool) Unclear call sites Argument labels, or an enum
"gold", "pending", "admin" strings Stringly-typed logic Enums
Several optionals that must be set together Invalid states are representable An enum with associated values, or a struct
Int IDs passed everywhere Primitive obsession Small wrapper types
! sprinkled through code Unhandled absence guard let, defaults, non-optional types
Deep class hierarchies Inheritance used for code reuse Protocols, composition
One change requires edits in ten files Scattered responsibility Move the knowledge into one type
Manager, Helper, Utils type names No clear responsibility Split by what each part actually does

When “clean” goes too far

Clean code is about making change cheaper, and abstractions have a cost too. Watch for:

  • A protocol with a single implementation and no test double. It’s indirection with no benefit; extract it when a second implementation or a test actually needs it.
  • Premature generalization. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Wait until the third copy, when you can see what really varies.
  • Clever code. Long chains of closures, custom operators, and dense one-liners can be shorter and still harder to read. Optimize for the reader.
  • Architecture by cargo cult. Five layers and a coordinator for a settings screen with two toggles isn’t clean; it’s ceremony.

Let the tools help

  • Compiler warnings are free code review; aim for zero, and treat new ones as errors in CI.
  • swift-format (included with the Swift 6 toolchain as swift format) or SwiftLint keep formatting consistent, so code reviews can focus on design.
  • Swift 6 language mode turns data races into compile errors.
  • Tests make refactoring safe, and refactoring is how code stays clean. The “boy scout rule” applies: leave each file a little better than you found it.

Interview questions

What does “clarity at the point of use” mean? APIs are designed so that call sites read clearly, because code is read far more often than it’s written: argument labels, role-based names, and mutating/non-mutating naming pairs like sort()/sorted().

How can Swift’s type system make invalid states unrepresentable? With enums that hold associated values for each state instead of independent flags and optionals, and with small wrapper types and failable initializers that validate data once.

Why are Boolean parameters considered a smell? They make call sites unreadable and can’t grow beyond two options. Argument labels help; enums are clearer and extensible.

When is an abstraction not worth it? When it has a single implementation, no test needs to replace it, and it only adds indirection. Introduce it when a real second use appears.

Summary

  • Clean code makes change cheap and safe; it isn’t about being short.
  • Name things for clarity at the call site; replace Boolean flags, strings, and primitive IDs with enums and small types.
  • Keep functions small, use guard for early exits, and make invalid states unrepresentable.
  • Prefer let, value types, final, and the most restrictive access level; avoid force-unwraps.
  • Put protocols in front of side effects, keep core logic pure, and handle errors explicitly.
  • Comment the why, avoid over-abstraction, and let the compiler, formatters, and tests keep the code honest.
entry.summary: Clean code is code that the next person, often you in six months, can read, trust, and change without fear. Most clean code advice is language-agnostic, but Swift gives you unusually strong tools to apply it: API design guidelines built around the call site, value types, optionals, enums with associated values, access control, and a compiler that can rule out whole classes of mistakes, including data races. This article starts with a realistic refactoring, then goes through the habits that make the biggest difference in day-to-day Swift, the code smells to watch for, and where “clean” turns into over-engineering.

entry.title: Swift Evolution: How the Language Changes

link.title: Swift Evolution: How the Language Changes

entry.content:
Every Swift feature you use, from async/await to if expressions to macros, went through a public process before it shipped. That process is Swift Evolution. Anyone can read the proposals, follow the debates, try the implementations, and take part. Knowing how it works pays off in very practical ways: proposals are the most precise documentation a feature has, their “alternatives considered” sections answer most “why didn’t they just…?” questions, and upcoming feature flags let you prepare your code for the next language mode years before it arrives. This article covers the process, its history, how to read a proposal, and how to use what’s coming in your own projects.

Swift Evolution: How the Language Changes

Where it happens

  • The swift-evolution repository on GitHub (swiftlang/swift-evolution) holds every proposal as a Markdown file, numbered SE-0001, SE-0002, and so on, with its current status.
  • The Swift Forums (forums.swift.org) host the discussions: early ideas under Evolution → Pitches, formal reviews under Evolution → Proposal Reviews, and the decisions, with their rationale, as announcements.
  • swift.org/swift-evolution offers a searchable dashboard of all proposals, filterable by status and by the Swift version that implemented them.

The life of a proposal

  1. Pitch. Someone posts an idea on the forums. The community discusses whether the problem is real and the direction is right. Most ideas are refined, merged with others, or dropped at this stage, and that’s the stage working well.
  2. Proposal. The idea is written up from the official template: motivation, proposed solution, detailed design, source compatibility, ABI compatibility, implications on adoption, and alternatives considered.
  3. Implementation. A working implementation is required before review, usually as a pull request against the compiler or standard library, often behind an experimental flag and available in a toolchain snapshot. That rule keeps reviews grounded: people can try the feature on real code, instead of debating a hypothetical.
  4. Review. The proposal is scheduled for a public review, typically around two weeks, run by a review manager from the group that owns the area. Anyone can post feedback. Reviewers are asked a few standard questions: Is the problem significant enough? Does the proposal fit the feel and direction of Swift? How does it compare with similar features in other languages? How much effort did you put into your review?
  5. Decision. The owning group announces one of: accepted, accepted with modifications, returned for revision (often followed by a second review), or rejected, always with a written rationale.
  6. Release. Accepted proposals ship in a future Swift version, and the status changes to “Implemented (Swift 5.9)”, for example.

Big features are usually split into several proposals. Swift concurrency, for example, was more than a dozen: async/await (SE-0296), structured concurrency (SE-0304), actors (SE-0306), Sendable (SE-0302), async let (SE-0317), and more, each reviewed separately, with vision documents describing how the pieces fit together.

A short history, told through proposals

Swift Evolution started when Swift went open source in December 2015, and its history explains a lot about the language’s priorities.

  • Swift 3 (2016): the great break. Early proposals made sweeping, source-breaking changes: removing ++ and -- (SE-0004), C-style for loops (SE-0007), and currying syntax (SE-0002), and renaming much of the Objective-C API surface (SE-0005, the “Grand Renaming”). The result was a much better language, and a painful migration for everyone.
  • Swift 4 and later: source compatibility. After Swift 3, source compatibility became a hard requirement. Breaking changes need an exceptionally strong reason and are grouped into language modes that each module adopts on its own schedule.
  • Swift 5 (2019): ABI stability, and module stability in 5.1, letting apps use the system’s Swift runtime instead of bundling their own; see ABI Stability.
  • Swift 5.5 to 5.10: concurrency, a multi-year series of proposals, delivered incrementally with warnings before errors.
  • Swift 6 (2024): data-race safety as a new language mode, the first major source-breaking change since Swift 3, and a fully opt-in one.

Some ideas don’t make it, and those decisions are just as instructive. SE-0217 proposed a !! “unwrap or die” operator; it was rejected, with the rationale that ?? fatalError("…") already expresses it in existing terms. Reading rejection rationales is one of the best ways to absorb what “Swifty” means to the people who design the language.

Reading a proposal

A proposal is useful long after the decision:

  • Motivation shows the problem, usually with the awkward code people had to write before. It’s the best way to understand when to use a feature.
  • Detailed design is the precise specification, more exact than most documentation: every rule, every edge case, and the grammar.
  • Source compatibility and ABI compatibility tell you whether you can adopt the feature in a library without breaking clients, and whether it needs a newer OS.
  • Alternatives considered explains rejected designs, which usually answers “why didn’t they just…?”
  • Future directions hints at what may come next.

Proposals worth reading alongside the features they describe, including the articles on this blog:

Proposal Feature Read with
SE-0258 Property wrappers Property Wrappers
SE-0296, SE-0306 async/await, actors Swift Concurrency
SE-0335 Existential any Opaque and Boxed Types
SE-0380 if and switch expressions Control Flow
SE-0382, SE-0389 Expression and attached macros Macros in Swift
SE-0386 The package access level Swift Package Manager
SE-0404 Nested protocols Nested Types
SE-0413 Typed throws Error Handling
SE-0414, SE-0430 Region-based isolation, sending Swift Concurrency

Language modes and source compatibility

A language mode is a set of source-breaking changes adopted together. A Swift 6 compiler supports Swift 4, 4.2, 5, and 6 modes, and you choose per module, so an app in Swift 6 mode can depend on a library still in Swift 5 mode, and vice versa:

// Package.swift
// .target(name: "LegacyKit", swiftSettings: [.swiftLanguageMode(.v5)])
//
// Xcode: Build Settings → Swift Language Version
// Command line: swiftc -swift-version 6

The compiler version and the language mode are different things, and conditional compilation can test both:

#if swift(>=6.0)
let languageModeNote = "Compiled in Swift 6 language mode or later"
#else
let languageModeNote = "Compiled in an older language mode"
#endif

#if compiler(>=6.0)
let compilerNote = "Built with a Swift 6 or newer compiler"
#else
let compilerNote = "Built with an older compiler"
#endif

print(languageModeNote)
print(compilerNote)

Built with a Swift 6 compiler in Swift 5 mode, this prints “older language mode” but “Swift 6 or newer compiler”. Library authors use #if compiler(>=…) to adopt new syntax while still supporting older toolchains, because #if swift only reflects the mode.

Upcoming features: the next mode, one change at a time

Every source-breaking change accepted for a future language mode gets an upcoming feature flag, so you can adopt it today, one change at a time, instead of all at once on migration day.

// Package.swift
// .target(
//     name: "App",
//     swiftSettings: [
//         .enableUpcomingFeature("ExistentialAny"),          // SE-0335
//         .enableUpcomingFeature("InternalImportsByDefault"), // SE-0409
//     ]
// )
//
// Xcode: Build Settings → "Upcoming Features", or Other Swift Flags:
//   -enable-upcoming-feature ExistentialAny

Code can check whether a feature is enabled with #if hasFeature(…):

#if hasFeature(ConciseMagicFile)
let fileNote = "#file is short, like Module/File.swift"
#else
let fileNote = "#file is a full path"
#endif
print(fileNote)

Here’s what some of these flags do. In Swift 5 mode, each is off unless you enable it; Swift 6 mode turns on most of them:

Flag Proposal What changes On in Swift 6 mode?
ConciseMagicFile SE-0274 #file becomes Module/File.swift instead of a full path (which leaked into binaries) Yes
BareSlashRegexLiterals SE-0354 /\d+/ is a regex literal Yes
StrictConcurrency SE-0337 Complete data-race checking Yes
ExistentialAny SE-0335 Using a protocol as a type must be spelled any P No (still upcoming)
InternalImportsByDefault SE-0409 import is internal unless marked public import No (still upcoming)

For example, let digits = /\d+/ fails to compile in Swift 5 mode (“’/’ is not a prefix unary operator”), and compiles once BareSlashRegexLiterals is enabled. With ExistentialAny enabled, let value: CustomStringConvertible = 42 is flagged: “use of protocol ‘CustomStringConvertible’ as a type must be written ‘any CustomStringConvertible’”.

A practical migration strategy for a new language mode:

  1. Enable the upcoming features one at a time, starting with the ones that produce the fewest diagnostics.
  2. Fix the code, commit, repeat.
  3. Switch the module to the new mode, which is now a small step.
  4. Do it module by module, leaf modules first.

Experimental features (.enableExperimentalFeature("…")) are different: they gate unfinished implementations that may change or disappear, and many only work with development toolchains. Don’t ship code that depends on them.

Who decides?

Swift is an open-source project with a published governance structure. The Core Team oversees the project as a whole and sets its strategy. Since 2022, specific areas belong to dedicated groups: a language steering group decides language and standard library proposals, and other workgroups and steering groups cover areas like the package ecosystem, platforms, documentation, and testing. Many members work at Apple, but reviews are public, decisions come with written rationales, and many accepted proposals are authored by community members.

How to take part

  • Read and follow proposals in areas you care about, and try them with a toolchain snapshot from swift.org or an Xcode beta.
  • Give feedback during reviews, especially concrete experience: “I tried this on a 200,000-line codebase, and here’s what happened” carries far more weight than opinions on syntax.
  • Pitch when you have a well-understood problem. Start with the problem and real-world examples, not the syntax, and search the forums first: many ideas were discussed before, and the “Commonly Rejected Changes” document lists the ones that keep coming back.
  • Contribute code or documentation. The Swift repositories label good first issues, and a proposal with an implementation moves much faster than one waiting for someone to build it.

Interview questions

What’s the difference between a Swift compiler version and a language mode? The compiler version is the toolchain (for example, Swift 6.0); the language mode is the set of source rules a module is compiled with. A Swift 6 compiler can build modules in Swift 5 mode. #if compiler tests the first, #if swift the second.

What are upcoming feature flags for? They let you adopt individual source-breaking changes planned for a future language mode ahead of time, making migration gradual.

Why does Swift group breaking changes into language modes? After the costly migrations of the Swift 3 era, source compatibility became a priority. Language modes let each module opt in on its own schedule, and modules in different modes work together.

Where would you look to understand why a Swift feature works the way it does? Its Swift Evolution proposal, especially the motivation, detailed design, and alternatives considered, plus the review thread and decision rationale on the forums.

Summary

  • Swift Evolution is the public process every language and standard library change goes through: pitch, proposal, implementation, review, decision.
  • Proposals live on GitHub as numbered SE documents and are reviewed on the Swift Forums; read them as precise documentation.
  • Since Swift 3, source compatibility is a priority: breaking changes are grouped into per-module language modes.
  • Upcoming feature flags and #if hasFeature let you adopt the next mode one change at a time; #if compiler and #if swift test different things.
  • Anyone can read, review, pitch, and contribute.
